title: Ἀετὸς καὶ κάνθαρος
part: The Eagle and the Beetle (Chambry 4 · Perry 3)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 4 (= Perry 3). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀετὸς λαγωὸν ἐδίωκεν· ὁ δὲ ἐν ἐρημίᾳ τῶν βοηθησόντων ὑπάρχων, ὃν μόνον ὁ καιρὸς παρέσχε, κάνθαρον ἰδών, τοῦτον ἱκέτευεν.
sentences.tr: Aetos lagōon ediōken· ho de en erēmiāi tōn boēthēsontōn hyparchōn, hon monon ho kairos paresche, kantharon idōn, touton hiketeuen.
sentences.l: An eagle was pursuing a hare; and he, being in a desert of those who would help, having seen a beetle — the only one the moment supplied — kept supplicating him.
sentences.i: An eagle was chasing a hare; and the hare, being in a wilderness so far as helpers went, caught sight of a beetle — the one helper the moment afforded — and fell to begging him.
sentences.n: τῶν βοηθησόντων is a future participle used as a noun, 'those who were going to help': the helpers that would have helped had there been any. The relative clause ὃν μόνον ὁ καιρὸς παρέσχε runs ahead of its own antecedent κάνθαρον, which Greek allows freely and English must reorder or set off with dashes. Both main verbs are imperfect: the chase and the pleading are still going on.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ παραθαρσύνας αὐτόν, ὡς ἐγγὺς ἐλθόντα τὸν ἀετὸν ἐθεάσατο, παρεκάλει μὴ ἀπάγειν αὐτοῦ τὸν ἱκέτην.
sentences.tr: Ho de paratharsynas auton, hōs engys elthonta ton aeton etheasato, parekalei mē apagein autou ton hiketēn.
sentences.l: And he, having encouraged him, when he saw the eagle having come near, kept urging him not to carry off his suppliant.
sentences.i: The beetle reassured him, and when he saw the eagle coming close, begged him not to carry off one who had taken refuge with him.
sentences.n: ἱκέτης, 'suppliant,' is a religious term, not a social one: whoever throws himself on another's protection stands under Zeus's own guardianship (Zeus Hikesios), so to refuse him is an offence against the god — which is why this fable ends in Zeus's lap. ἐθεάσατο takes a participle as its complement (ἐλθόντα), 'saw the eagle having come near': verbs of perceiving take the participle where verbs of saying take the infinitive.

sentences.t: Κἀκεῖνος ὑπεριδὼν τὴν μικρότητα ἐν ὄψει τοῦ κανθάρου τὸν λαγωὸν κατεθοινήσατο.
sentences.tr: Kakeinos hyperidōn tēn mikrotēta en opsei tou kantharou ton lagōon katethoinēsato.
sentences.l: And that one, having looked down on the smallness, in the sight of the beetle feasted upon the hare.
sentences.i: But the eagle, scorning so small a creature, devoured the hare before the beetle's very eyes.
sentences.n: Κἀκεῖνος is crasis, καὶ ἐκεῖνος fused into one word; the mark over the alpha is the coronis, not a breathing. τὴν μικρότητα, 'the smallness,' with the article — the beetle's known quality, and the thing the whole fable is about.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἀπ’ ἐκείνου μνησικακῶν διετέλει παρατηρούμενος τοῦ ἀετοῦ τὰς καλιὰς καί, εἴ ποτε ἐκεῖνος ἔτικτε, μετάρσιος αἰρόμενος ἐκύλιε τὰ ὠὰ καὶ κατέασσε, μέχρις οὗ πανταχόθεν ἐλαυνόμενος ὁ ἀετὸς ἐπὶ τὸν Δία κατέφυγεν (ἐστὶ δὲ τοῦ Διὸς ἱερὸς ὁ ὄρνις), καὶ αὐτοῦ ἐδεήθη τόπον αὐτῷ πρὸς νεοττοποιίαν ἀσφαλῆ παρασχεῖν.
sentences.tr: Ho de ap’ ekeinou mnēsikakōn dietelei paratēroumenos tou aetou tas kalias kai, ei pote ekeinos etikte, metarsios airomenos ekylie ta ōa kai kateasse, mechris hou pantachothen elaunomenos ho aetos epi ton Dia katephygen (esti de tou Dios hieros ho ornis), kai autou edeēthē topon autōi pros neottopoiian asphalē paraschein.
sentences.l: And he from that time on, bearing the grudge, continued watching the eagle's nests, and, if ever that one laid, rising high in the air he would roll the eggs out and smash them, until the eagle, driven from every side, took refuge with Zeus (the bird is sacred to Zeus), and begged him to furnish him a place safe for nest-making.
sentences.i: From that day the beetle nursed his grievance and never left off watching the eagle's nests; whenever the eagle laid, he would rise into the air, roll the eggs out and break them, until the eagle, harried from every quarter, fled to Zeus — the eagle is Zeus's own sacred bird — and begged him to provide a safe place to raise its young.
sentences.n: διετέλει with a participle, 'he continued watching': a supplementary participle where English says 'kept on -ing.' The imperfects ἔτικτε, ἐκύλιε, κατέασσε are iterative — this happened again and again, not once. μέχρις οὗ is 'until.' The parenthesis is the fable's own footnote, and it is load-bearing: because the eagle is Zeus's bird, Zeus is the one refuge left, and the beetle's revenge reaches even there. ἐδεήθη (δέομαι) takes the genitive of the person asked, αὐτοῦ. Note that the eagle stays grammatically masculine (ἐκεῖνος, ὁ ἀετός) even while laying eggs: Greek follows the gender of the noun, not of the creature.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ Διὸς ἐν τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ κόλποις τίκτειν ἐπιτρέψαντος αὐτῷ, ὁ κάνθαρος τοῦτο ἑωρακώς, κόπρου σφαῖραν ποιήσας, ἀνέπτη καὶ γενόμενος κατὰ τοὺς τοῦ Διὸς κόλπους ἐνταῦθα καθῆκεν.
sentences.tr: Tou de Dios en tois heautou kolpois tiktein epitrepsantos autōi, ho kantharos touto heōrakōs, koprou sphairan poiēsas, aneptē kai genomenos kata tous tou Dios kolpous entautha kathēken.
sentences.l: And Zeus having permitted him to lay in his own lap, the beetle, having seen this, having made a ball of dung, flew up and, having come to be over Zeus's lap, dropped it there.
sentences.i: Zeus allowed the eagle to lay in the fold of his own robe; and the beetle, having seen this, made a ball of dung, flew up, and when he was directly above Zeus's lap, let it fall.
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute (Τοῦ Διὸς … ἐπιτρέψαντος), and then three participles before the first finite verb. κόλπος is the fold of a garment at the breast, hence a lap — the safest place in the world, which is the point. The dung ball is the beetle's own nature put to use: the scarab rolls one wherever it goes. κατά with the accusative here is 'down opposite, right over.'

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ Ζεὺς ἀποσείσασθαι τὴν κόπρον βουλόμενος, ὡς διανέστη, ἔλαθεν τὰ ὠὰ ἀπορρίψας.
sentences.tr: Ho de Zeus aposeisasthai tēn kopron boulomenos, hōs dianestē, elathen ta ōa aporripsas.
sentences.l: And Zeus, wishing to shake off the dung, when he stood up, escaped his own notice having thrown out the eggs.
sentences.i: Zeus, wanting to shake the dung off, stood up — and threw out the eggs without noticing.
sentences.n: λανθάνω with a participle, the classic Greek inversion: 'he escaped notice having thrown out the eggs' = he threw them out without noticing. The event sits in the participle and the manner in the finite verb, the reverse of the English arrangement; you will meet it constantly.

sentences.t: Ἀπ’ ἐκείνου τέ φασι περὶ ὃν καιρὸν οἱ κάνθαροι γίγνονται μὴ νεοττεύειν τοὺς ἀετούς.
sentences.tr: Ap’ ekeinou te phasi peri hon kairon hoi kantharoi gignontai mē neotteuein tous aetous.
sentences.l: And from that time, they say, at the season in which the beetles come to be, the eagles do not nest.
sentences.n: φασί introduces indirect discourse with accusative and infinitive: μὴ νεοττεύειν τοὺς ἀετούς, 'that the eagles do not nest.' περὶ ὃν καιρόν is an incorporated relative — the antecedent has been pulled inside its own clause — 'about which season' for 'at the season at which.' An aetiological ending: the fable closes by explaining a fact of the natural calendar, as many Greek stories do.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος διδάσκει μηδενὸς καταφρονεῖν λογιζομένους ὅτι οὐδεὶς οὕτως ἐστὶν ἀδύνατος ὡς προπηλακισθεὶς μὴ δύνασθαί ποτε ἑαυτὸν ἐκδικῆσαι.
sentences.tr: Ho logos didaskei mēdenos kataphronein logizomenous hoti oudeis houtōs estin adynatos hōs propēlakistheis mē dynasthai pote heauton ekdikēsai.
sentences.l: The story teaches to despise no one, reckoning that no one is so powerless as, having been insulted, not to be able ever to avenge himself.
sentences.i: The story teaches us to despise no one, reckoning that no one is so powerless that, once he has been abused, he can never avenge himself.
sentences.n: A closing formula outside the usual set: ὁ λόγος διδάσκει, 'the story teaches…', taking an infinitive rather than the ὅτι-clause of ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι. καταφρονέω takes the genitive, μηδενός. οὕτως … ὡς with the infinitive is a result construction, 'so … as to.' λογιζομένους is accusative, agreeing with the unexpressed 'us' who are the subject of καταφρονεῖν — Greek leaves that subject out and lets the case of the participle imply it.
